message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"12.21","text":"When Peter had said these things, the woman stopped and, as though from shock, fainted. Peter came over and paused, then urged her to recover a clear mind, trying to persuade her to say what exactly was happening to her. As though recovering from drunkenness, with the rest of her body gone limp, she regained control of herself so that she could bear the magnitude of the joy she was anticipating. Rubbing her face, she said, “Where is this young man?” Peter, who by now had discerned the whole situation, said, “You tell me first (for otherwise you have no way to see him)—.” In her eagerness she said, “I am the young man’s mother.” Peter said, “What is his name?” She replied, “Clement.” Peter said, “It is he. He was the one who spoke with me a short while ago, whom I instructed to wait for me in the ship.” Falling at Peter’s feet, she begged him to hurry to the ship. Peter said, “If you keep our agreement, I will do this too.” She said, “I will do everything; only show me my only child, for through him I will seem to see my two children who died here.” Peter said, “When you see him, remain quiet until we have left the island.” She said, “I will do so.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἐπιστήσασα ὡς ὑπὸ ἐκπλήξεως ἀπέψυξεν","chosen":"stopped and, as though from shock, fainted","rationale":"ἐπιστήσασα marks her coming to a halt, while ἀπέψυξεν here describes a collapse or loss of consciousness rather than literal death."},{"source_quote":"ἐπισχὼν νήφειν αὐτὴν παρεκελεύσατο","chosen":"paused, then urged her to recover a clear mind","rationale":"The absolute ἐπισχών can mean that Peter paused or waited; alternatively, the context may suggest that he supported or steadied her. νήφειν denotes recovering mental clarity."},{"source_quote":"ἡ δὲ ὥσπερ ἐκ μέθης τὸ λοιπὸν τοῦ σώματος παρεθεῖσα","chosen":"As though recovering from drunkenness, with the rest of her body gone limp","rationale":"ἐκ preserves the image of emerging from drunkenness, while the participial phrase depicts the remaining bodily weakness accompanying her recovery."},{"source_quote":"ὑπέστρεψεν ἑαυτὴν ὑποστῆναι δυνηθῆναι","chosen":"she regained control of herself so that she could bear","rationale":"The unusual sequence presents her as recovering sufficiently to withstand the anticipated joy; more formally, she “turned herself back” so as to be able to endure it."},{"source_quote":"Εἰπέ μοι σὺ πρῶτον","chosen":"You tell me first","rationale":"No object of “tell” is expressed. The translation preserves the incomplete prompt rather than supplying what Peter requires her to tell him."},{"source_quote":"Εἴ μοι τηρεῖς τὰς συνθήκας","chosen":"If you keep our agreement","rationale":"συνθήκας denotes agreed terms or conditions, referring to Peter’s requirement that she remain composed."},{"source_quote":"τὸ τέκνον τὸ μονογενὲς","chosen":"my only child","rationale":"μονογενές presents Clement as her unique or sole remaining child in this context; “only-born child” would misleadingly conflict with the immediately mentioned deceased children."},{"source_quote":"δόξω γὰρ δι’ αὐτοῦ τὰ δύο μου τὰ ἐνταῦθα τεθνηκότα ὁρᾶν τέκνα","chosen":"for through him I will seem to see my two children who died here","rationale":"δόξω with the infinitive is preserved as “I will seem to see,” expressing how seeing Clement will represent the two deceased children to her."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"Εἰπέ μοι σὺ πρῶτον (ἄλλως γὰρ τοῦτον ἰδεῖν οὐκ ἔχεις) —.","issue":"The selected edition prints a terminal dash after Peter’s unfinished prompt and before the period. It may signal interrupted or deliberately incomplete speech, or it may be an editorial marker, but its function is uncertain. The marker is retained, and no unexpressed object or completion has been supplied.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"12.22","text":"Peter therefore took her by the hand and led her toward the ship. When I saw him leading a woman by the hand, I laughed; and I came over and, out of respect for him, tried to lead her in his place. The moment I touched her hand, she gave a great cry like a mother, wrapped herself around me, and fervently showered me, her own son, with kisses. Knowing nothing of the whole situation, I was trying to shake her off as though she were mad; yet, feeling deference toward Peter as well, I was becoming irritated.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"εἰς τιμὴν αὐτοῦ ἀντ’ αὐτοῦ χειραγωγεῖν αὐτὴν ἐπειρώμην","chosen":"out of respect for him, tried to lead her in his place","rationale":"Clement attempts to relieve Peter of the task as an expression of honor or respect."},{"source_quote":"ὀλολύξασα ὡς μήτηρ μέγα","chosen":"she gave a great cry like a mother","rationale":"ὀλολύζω denotes a loud, emotionally charged cry; the comparison explicitly characterizes it as maternal."},{"source_quote":"περιπλακεῖσα σφόδρα κατεφίλει με","chosen":"wrapped herself around me, and fervently showered me with kisses","rationale":"περιπλέκομαι describes an enclosing embrace, while the intensive καταφιλέω conveys repeated or ardent kissing."},{"source_quote":"με τὸν αὐτῆς υἱόν","chosen":"me, her own son","rationale":"The accusative phrase stands in apposition to με and identifies Clement as her son from the mother’s perspective."},{"source_quote":"ὡς μαινομένην ἀπεσειόμην","chosen":"I was trying to shake her off as though she were mad","rationale":"The imperfect depicts the ongoing or attempted action that Peter addresses with ἀποσειόμενος in the following section, rather than a completed dismissal."},{"source_quote":"αἰδούμενος δὲ καὶ τὸν Πέτρον ἐπικραινόμην","chosen":"yet, feeling deference toward Peter as well, I was becoming irritated","rationale":"αἰδέομαι with Peter as its object expresses regard or deference; the imperfect ἐπικραινόμην describes Clement’s developing vexation."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"12.23","text":"Peter said, “Let her be! What are you doing, child Clement, shaking off the woman who truly gave birth to you?” When I heard this, I became covered in tears; and I threw myself upon the woman who had borne me, who had herself fallen down, and showered her with kisses. For as soon as this was said to me, I somehow began dimly to recall her appearance. Many crowds therefore came running to learn about the woman who had been begging, saying to one another, “Her son, a man of distinction, has recognized her.” When we wished to leave the island at once with my mother, she said, “My longed-for child, it is right to say farewell to the woman who took me in. She is poor and completely disabled and lies at home.” When Peter heard this, he marveled, as did all the surrounding crowds, at the woman’s noble disposition. Peter immediately ordered some men to go and carry the woman in on a cot. And likewise, when she had been brought in and the cot had been set down, Peter said in the hearing of all the crowds, “If I am indeed a herald of truth, then, as grounds for faith among those standing by, so that they may know that there is one God, the one who made the world, let her rise immediately in health.” As soon as Peter said this, the woman rose, having been healed. She fell before Peter, and after showering her familiar friend with kisses, she asked what this might mean. Her friend briefly related to her the whole event of the recognition, and those who heard it were astounded. Then the mother, seeing that her hostess had been healed, asked that she too might receive healing. Peter laid his hand on her and healed her as well.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἀποσειόμενος τὴν σὴν ὄντως τεκοῦσαν","chosen":"shaking off the woman who truly gave birth to you","rationale":"ὄντως emphasizes that she is genuinely Clement’s birth mother, while the present participle recalls his ongoing attempt to push her away."},{"source_quote":"περίδακρυς γενόμενος","chosen":"I became covered in tears","rationale":"περίδακρυς depicts Clement as streaming with tears."},{"source_quote":"καταπεσούσῃ τῇ τεκούσῃ προσπεσὼν","chosen":"I threw myself upon the woman who had borne me, who had herself fallen down","rationale":"The participles distinguish the mother’s prior collapse from Clement’s movement toward and onto her."},{"source_quote":"ἀμαυρῶς πως τὸ εἶδος ἀνεκαλούμην","chosen":"I somehow began dimly to recall her appearance","rationale":"ἀμαυρῶς marks the memory as indistinct, and the imperfect suggests an emerging recollection."},{"source_quote":"ἱστορῆσαι τὴν προσαιτήτριαν γυναῖκα","chosen":"to learn about the woman who had been begging","rationale":"ἱστορέω here can mean to investigate, inquire about, or learn the story of someone; “to see” is also possible but expresses the crowds’ curiosity less fully."},{"source_quote":"ὅλη παρειμένη","chosen":"completely disabled","rationale":"The passive description indicates that her body has lost its strength or function; “completely paralyzed” is a possible narrower rendering."},{"source_quote":"καὶ ὁμῶς ἐνεχθείσης","chosen":"And likewise, when she had been brought in","rationale":"ὁμῶς is unusual here but can bear the sense “likewise” or “similarly”; the translation does not replace it with the more expected ὅμως."},{"source_quote":"εἰς τὴν τῶν παρεστώτων πίστιν","chosen":"as grounds for faith among those standing by","rationale":"The phrase presents the healing as serving or producing the faith of those present."},{"source_quote":"τὴν συνήθη φίλην","chosen":"her familiar friend","rationale":"συνήθης identifies Clement’s mother as the healed woman’s accustomed or close associate."},{"source_quote":"τὴν ξενοδόχον θεραπευθεῖσαν ἱστορήσασα","chosen":"seeing that her hostess had been healed","rationale":"Here ἱστορέω is understood as observing or ascertaining the hostess’s healed condition; “having inquired about the healed hostess” remains possible."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"12.24","text":"And then, in this way, Peter spoke about God and the worship that belongs to him, adding at the end: “If anyone wishes to learn these things accurately, let him come to Antioch, where I have decided to remain for several days, and learn the things that lead to his salvation. For surely it cannot be that you know how to leave your homelands for commerce or military service and travel to distant places, yet are unwilling to undertake even a three-day journey for eternal salvation.” After Peter’s address, in the presence of the entire crowd, I gave the woman who had been healed one thousand drachmas for provisions and entrusted her to a certain good man who was the foremost citizen of the city and was naturally disposed to do this with joy. After also distributing money to many others and thanking the women who had once comforted my mother, I sailed across to Antaradus together with my mother, Peter, and the remaining companions; and in this way we made our way to our lodging.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τῆς αὐτῷ διαφερούσης θρησκείας","chosen":"the worship that belongs to him","rationale":"διαφέρειν with the dative can denote what pertains or is proper to someone; θρησκεία here is religious worship or observance."},{"source_quote":"τὰ πρὸς τὴν αὐτοῦ σωτηρίαν","chosen":"the things that lead to his salvation","rationale":"πρός expresses relation or direction toward the hearer’s salvation."},{"source_quote":"οὐ γὰρ δὴ ἐμπορίας ἕνεκα ἢ στρατείας πατρίδας καταλιμπάνειν οἴδατε καὶ εἰς μακροὺς ἀπέρχεσθαι τόπους","chosen":"For surely it cannot be that you know how to leave your homelands for commerce or military service and travel to distant places","rationale":"The initial οὐ is retained as a rhetorical rejection of the inconsistent behavior Peter describes. Alternatively, the clause may be punctuated as a direct rhetorical question: “Do you not know how to leave ...?”"},{"source_quote":"διὰ δὲ αἰώνιον σωτηρίαν μηδὲ τριῶν ἡμερῶν ὁδὸν πορευθῆναι θέλειν","chosen":"yet are unwilling to undertake even a three-day journey for eternal salvation","rationale":"The rendering preserves the contrast and the negative force of μηδέ while expressing the syntactically abrupt infinitive θέλειν as part of the rhetorical rejection introduced by οὐ."},{"source_quote":"πρώτῳ τῆς πόλεως ὄντι","chosen":"the foremost citizen of the city","rationale":"πρῶτος describes the man’s leading civic standing, not merely his chronological position."},{"source_quote":"φύσει μετὰ χαρᾶς τοῦτο ποιεῖν προῃρημένῳ","chosen":"was naturally disposed to do this with joy","rationale":"προαιρεῖσθαι here denotes settled willingness or inclination, qualified by φύσει."},{"source_quote":"εἰς Ἀντάραδον","chosen":"to Antaradus","rationale":"Antaradus is the conventional English form of the place-name Ἀντάραδος."},{"source_quote":"εἰς τὴν ξενίαν ὡρμήσαμεν","chosen":"we made our way to our lodging","rationale":"ξενία denotes guest lodging or quarters, and ὁρμάω here means to set out or proceed toward them."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"διὰ δὲ αἰώνιον σωτηρίαν μηδὲ τριῶν ἡμερῶν ὁδὸν πορευθῆναι θέλειν","issue":"The infinitive θέλειν is syntactically abrupt where a finite verb would make the contrast straightforward. The verified supplied reading remains intelligible as an anacoluthon within the preceding rhetorical construction and has been preserved in translation.","proposed_reading":"διὰ δὲ αἰώνιον σωτηρίαν μηδὲ τριῶν ἡμερῶν ὁδὸν πορευθῆναι θέλετε","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"12.25","text":"When we had arrived ... and had partaken of food and given thanks as usual, while there was still time, I said to Peter, “My lord Peter, my mother performed an act of love for humanity when she remembered the woman who had hosted her.” Peter answered, “Do you really think, Clement, that the woman who bore you has performed an act of love for humanity, in that she repaid the woman who received her after the shipwreck? Or did you make this statement as one bestowing a great favor on your mother? If, however, you spoke not as one showing favor but as one telling the truth, you seem to me not to understand what the greatness of love for humanity actually is. It is affection for anyone at all, insofar as that person is human, without anything that naturally prompts it. Nor do I dare call the hostess who received the woman who bore you after the shipwreck a lover of humanity on that account. For, cajoled by pity, she had been persuaded to become the benefactor of a woman who had suffered shipwreck, was mourning children, was a foreigner, was naked, was alone, and was bitterly lamenting her disasters. Since she was amid so many disasters, who, even among the impious, would not have pitied her on seeing her? Consequently, even the hostess does not appear to have performed in this way an act of love for humanity, but to have acted under pity that had been stirred toward benefaction by countless disasters. How much more, then, did the woman who bore you—after acquiring abundant means and repaying her hostess—perform an act not of love for humanity, but of friendship? There is a great difference between friendship and love for humanity: friendship arises from repayment, whereas love for humanity, without anything that naturally prompts it, loves and benefits every human being insofar as that one is human. If, then, the hostess who showed pity had also pitied and benefited enemies who had wronged her, she would have been a lover of humanity. But if the enemy is a friend for some reason and the friend is an enemy for some reason, such a person is a friend or enemy of some particular cause, not of the human being.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"γενομένων δὲ ἡμῶν ...","chosen":"When we had arrived ...","rationale":"γενομένων ἡμῶν can describe the party’s arrival or presence, but the printed lacuna removes its following specification; the three dots are retained without restoration."},{"source_quote":"Φιλανθρωπίας ἔργον","chosen":"an act of love for humanity","rationale":"The expanded rendering preserves the etymological and argumentative connection among φιλανθρωπία, φιλάνθρωπος, and the later contrast with φιλία."},{"source_quote":"ὡς μητρὶ μεγάλα χαριζόμενος","chosen":"as one bestowing a great favor on your mother","rationale":"Peter asks whether Clement’s judgment was an indulgent compliment to his mother rather than a true classification of her act."},{"source_quote":"ἡ ἄνευ τοῦ φυσικῶς πείθοντος πρὸς οἱονδήποτε στοργὴ καθὸ ἄνθρωπός ἐστιν","chosen":"affection for anyone at all, insofar as that person is human, without anything that naturally prompts it","rationale":"Peter defines love for humanity as affection grounded solely in the recipient’s humanity, without a natural or circumstantial inducement."},{"source_quote":"ὑπ’ ἐλέου γὰρ κολακευθεῖσα","chosen":"For, cajoled by pity","rationale":"The rendering retains the personifying force of κολακεύω: pity flatters, coaxes, or cajoles the hostess into action."},{"source_quote":"ὑπὸ ἐλέου τοῦ ἐπὶ μυρίαις συμφοραῖς πρὸς εὐεργεσίας κεκινημένου","chosen":"under pity that had been stirred toward benefaction by countless disasters","rationale":"The genitive participle most naturally modifies ἐλέου, personifying pity itself as moved toward doing good by the accumulation of misfortunes."},{"source_quote":"ἡ μὲν φιλία ἐξ ἀμοιβῆς γίνεται","chosen":"friendship arises from repayment","rationale":"ἀμοιβή can mean repayment, return, or reciprocity; “repayment” keeps the immediate connection with the mother’s recompense to her hostess."},{"source_quote":"εἰ δὲ διὰ τί φίλη ἡ ἐχθρὰ καὶ διὰ τί ἐχθρὰ ἡ φίλη","chosen":"But if the enemy is a friend for some reason and the friend is an enemy for some reason","rationale":"διὰ τί may be interrogative, “why,” or causal, “for some reason.” The causal reading best continues the contrast between unconditional regard for a human being and attachment produced by a particular cause."},{"source_quote":"ἡ τοιαύτη τοῦ τινὸς αἰτίου φίλη ἐστὶν ἢ ἐχθρά, οὐ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου","chosen":"such a person is a friend or enemy of some particular cause, not of the human being","rationale":"The rendering preserves the source’s compressed genitive contrast. Alternatively, it may mean that such a person is friend or enemy because of some particular cause, not because the other is human."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"γενομένων δὲ ἡμῶν ...","issue":"The selected edition prints exactly three dots after γενομένων δὲ ἡμῶν, marking unavailable content. The gap is retained exactly in the English, and no restoration has been supplied.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"φιλανθρωπίας. ἔργον","issue":"The printed period interrupts the phrase φιλανθρωπίας ἔργον. It has been treated provisionally as editorial punctuation rather than as a syntactic break; no Greek word has been altered.","proposed_reading":"φιλανθρωπίας ἔργον","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"φιλάνθρωπος ἂν. ἦν.","issue":"The printed period separates the modal particle ἄν from the verb ἦν. The translation provisionally reads the words continuously as a normal contrary-to-fact construction while preserving every printed word.","proposed_reading":"φιλάνθρωπος ἂν ἦν.","blocks_publication":false}]}]}
